White sturgeon (Acipenser transmontanus) embryos incubated at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] exhibit a predictable developmental chronology, with eclosion occurring after approximately 8.75 days . This hatching interval, observed under controlled laboratory conditions, is notably brief compared to other Acipenseriformes and reflects the relatively high incubation temperature employed. Following chorion rupture, the resultant yolk-sac larvae commence their endotrophic phase, relying entirely on endogenous reserves. The transition to exogenous nutrition, marked by yolk-sac resorption and mouth opening, typically occurs at an age of approximately 15.75 days [ab = approximately 15.75 days], or roughly 7 days after hatch, representing the onset of first feeding at a time when the prolarvae measure approximately 1.2 centimeters [Lb = approximately 1.2 centimeters] at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This length at first feeding is consistent across rearing studies, establishing a baseline for early growth trajectories.

Field surveys and mark-recapture studies across the Columbia River basin have documented that White sturgeon achieve sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gametogenesis and gonadal recrudescence, after a protracted juvenile phase. Reproductive output in this large-bodied, iteroparous species is substantial, reflecting a life-history strategy geared toward high fecundity. The spawning runs typically occur when water temperatures are around 13 °C [T = 13 °C], a thermal cue that synchronizes gamete release across the population.

Adult White sturgeon are among the largest freshwater fishes in North America, achieving extraordinary dimensions over their extended lifespans. The maximum recorded total length is 610 centimeters [Li = 610 centimeters], though individuals of this size are encountered only rarely in contemporary surveys, with a common total length of 210 centimeters being far more typical across most populations. Corresponding to this ultimate length, the ultimate wet weight of the species reaches approximately 816,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 816,000 grams], representing the asymptotic mass approached by the oldest and largest individuals. The enormous size disparity from the neonatal stage is underscored by a direct comparison: a larva at first feeding weighs only about 0.0224 grams [Wwb = about 0.0224 grams], meaning a fully grown adult can attain a mass over 36 million times greater. This prodigious growth is sustained over a maximum lifespan of approximately 39,420 days [am = approximately 39,420 days], or roughly 108 years, making this one of the longest-lived of all teleost species at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C].

Body mass continues to increase with length throughout the adult phase, and empirical weight-length relationships derived from extensive sampling provide reliable predictors. For example, an individual measuring 290 centimeters in total length has a predicted wet weight at TL 290 cm of approximately 225,000 grams . This allometric relationship is consistent with the robust, fusiform body plan of Acipenser transmontanus. The accumulation of such mass over a life span that, under the thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], extends to roughly 108 years [am = roughly 108 years], illustrates a remarkably slow pace of life. Mortality in the oldest individuals is primarily attributable to senescence and the progressive failure of physiological homeostasis, with natural mortality being the dominant endpoint for those that evade fishing pressure. Comparative data from other North American sturgeon species indicate that such longevity and extreme body size are derived traits within the family Acipenseridae.
